meaning-in-life.name: Meaning in life
meaning-in-life.line: I don't know what my life is for.

sources.passage: Nearly 3 in 5 young adults (58%) reported that they lacked “meaning or purpose” in their lives in the previous month.
Almost 1 in 10 adults (9%) reported low levels of feeling that the things they do in life are worthwhile; this was more common among adults aged 16 to 29 years (14%) and 30 to 49 years (11%).

meaning-in-life.prevalence: 58% of U.S. young adults said they lacked meaning or purpose in the previous month (Harvard Making Caring Common). In Great Britain, 9% of adults report low levels of feeling that what they do is worthwhile, 14% among those aged 16 to 29 (ONS).

dont-know-what-i-want.name: What I want
dont-know-what-i-want.line: I don't know what I want to do with my life.
aliases: Not knowing what to do with my life

sources.passage: Half of young adults reported that their mental health was negatively influenced by “not knowing what to do with my life.”

dont-know-what-i-want.prevalence: Half of U.S. young adults said "not knowing what to do with my life" hurt their mental health (Harvard Making Caring Common).

reading.name: Reading
reading.line: Reading forms, letters and instructions is hard for me.

sources.passage: Between 2017 and 2023, there were increases in the percentages of adults performing at the lowest proficiency level (Level 1 or below) in both literacy and numeracy: in literacy this percentage increased from 19 to 28 percent and in numeracy from 29 to 34 percent.
The average rate of literacy needs across the OECD is 26%

reading.prevalence: 28 percent of U.S. adults read at Level 1 or below, up from 19 percent in 2017 (NCES, PIAAC 2023). The OECD average is 26%.

everyday-math.name: Math
everyday-math.line: Everyday math, like working out a bill or a discount, is hard for me.

sources.passage: Between 2017 and 2023, there were increases in the percentages of adults performing at the lowest proficiency level (Level 1 or below) in both literacy and numeracy: in literacy this percentage increased from 19 to 28 percent and in numeracy from 29 to 34 percent.
The average rate of numeracy needs across the OECD is 25%.

everyday-math.prevalence: 34 percent of U.S. adults are at Level 1 or below in numeracy, up from 29 percent in 2017 (NCES, PIAAC 2023). The OECD average is 25%.

computers.name: Computers
computers.line: I struggle to do things on a computer or phone that everyone now expects.

sources.passage: About 16 percent of U.S. adults are not digitally literate, compared to 23 percent of adults internationally.

computers.prevalence: About 16 percent of U.S. adults are not digitally literate, compared to 23 percent internationally (NCES/AIR, PIAAC).

english.name: English
english.line: I don't speak English well enough to get by.

sources.passage: Over three-quarters (78.3%) of the nation age 5 and older spoke only English at home, according to newly released 2018-2022 American Community Survey (ACS), 5-year estimates.

Among the population age 5 and older that spoke a language other than English at home, 61.0% of Spanish speakers, 48.2% of Chinese speakers (which includes all dialects), and 69.8% of Tagalog (including Filipino) speakers spoke English “very well.”

english.prevalence: In 2018-2022, 78.3% of U.S. residents age 5 and older spoke only English at home. Among those who spoke another language, 61.0% of Spanish speakers and 48.2% of Chinese speakers spoke English "very well" (Census ACS).

diploma.name: Diploma
diploma.line: I never finished high school, and it holds me back.

sources.passage: In 2022, the highest level of education of the population age 25 and older in the United States ranged from less than high school to advanced degrees beyond a bachelor’s degree. 9% had less than a high school diploma or equivalent.

diploma.prevalence: In 2022, 9% of U.S. adults age 25 and older had less than a high school diploma or equivalent (Census Bureau).

no-time-to-learn.name: Classes
no-time-to-learn.line: I want to take a class or training, but I can't fit it around work, family or money.

sources.passage: Of those who wanted to participate and could not (10.2%) or those who participated but wanted to participate more (15.7%), 25.3% listed training schedules as the main barrier to their participation, while 16.0% cited family reasons, and 15.2% highlighted costs

no-time-to-learn.prevalence: Among EU adults who wanted more education or training, 25.3% named schedules as the main barrier, 16.0% family reasons and 15.2% costs (European Commission employment and social developments report).
